blocks.text: The letter opens with a figure identifying himself only as 'the elder,' using a title rather than a personal name. He addresses the recipient as 'the elect lady'—a metaphor for a community—and her children. The elder's love encompasses not only the addressees but all who know the truth, signaling that his concern is rooted in shared theological conviction.

Truth holds enduring place in the elder's theology. It remains within sender and addressees and will be with them forever. This permanence grounds the blessing that follows: grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Jesus Christ, the Father's Son—both rooted in truth and love.

The elder rejoices to learn that some of the lady's children are walking in truth—a phrase denoting conduct aligned with a command received from the Father. This report provides grounds for confidence, though it may also imply that not all children are doing so.

The elder frames his plea as an appeal to something already established: not a new commandment, but one held from the beginning. That commandment is love—defined concretely as walking according to God's commandments. Love is thus bound up with obedience, not sentiment.

A grave threat has emerged: many deceivers have gone out into the world. The elder identifies them by a single marker—they refuse to confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. This denial is not incidental; the elder labels such a person 'the deceiver and the antichrist.' The embodied incarnation is foundational to right confession of Christ.

Between identifying the threat and responding to it, the elder calls for vigilance. The addressees are told to watch themselves so that the work accomplished among them is not lost and so that they may receive a full reward. This exhortation assumes the community's spiritual gains remain at risk.

The elder gives explicit practical instruction: anyone who comes without this teaching is not to be received into the house and must not be given a greeting. These acts—reception and greeting—were markers of hospitality and communion in the ancient world. By withholding them, the community enforces a boundary. The elder explains that to greet such a person is to share in their evil works, making hospitality itself a form of complicity.

The elder has much more to communicate but chooses not to do so by paper and ink. Instead, he expresses hope for a face-to-face meeting where joy may be completed by direct speaking. This shift reflects the preference for oral communication in the ancient world and suggests the gravity and sensitivity of matters at hand.
The letter closes with greetings from the children of the addressee's elect sister, extending the web of familial and spiritual relationship that frames the letter's concerns.
